name: Amasai
title: Leader of the warriors who joined David
summary: When David was staying in Ziklag during his persecution by King Saul, a group of warriors from the tribes of Benjamin and Judah came to join him. Their leader Amasai was filled with God's Spirit and spoke prophetic words of loyalty: "We are yours, David! We stand with you, son of Jesse! Peace, peace be upon you, and peace be upon your helpers! For your God helps you." These inspiring words convinced David that they came in good faith, and he gave them leadership positions among his warriors. This episode highlights the divine guidance behind the support for David and marks Amasai as an instrument of the Spirit's voice during a politically and spiritually decisive transition period in Israel's history.

keyEvents.title: Warriors from Benjamin and Judah come to David
keyEvents.description: A group of warriors from the tribes of Benjamin and Judah came to David while he was staying in Ziklag. David went out to meet them and challenged them to declare whether they had come in peace or as enemies.

keyEvents.title: The Spirit comes upon Amasai, and he declares loyalty
keyEvents.description: The Spirit came upon Amasai, the leader of the group, and he proclaimed loyalty to David with inspired words: "We are yours, David! We stand with you, son of Jesse! Peace, peace be with you, and peace with your helpers! For your God helps you." David then received them and appointed them as leaders among his warriors.

versions.summary: Amasai was the leader of a group of thirty warriors who came to David in Ziklag while he was fleeing from King Saul. The Holy Spirit came upon Amasai, and he declared loyalty to David with inspired words. He may also be identical to Amasa, one of David's commanders, although this is debated among biblical scholars.
versions.title: Leader of the thirty warriors
versions.reason: [major] The title contains a spelling error: 'krigerene' should be 'krigerne'. Additionally, 1 Chronicles 12:18 describes Amasai as 'leader of the thirty' (or 'head of the captains'), not necessarily 'the thirty warriors' as a fixed group. The text states that the Spirit came upon Amasai who was 'captain of the thirty', but this likely refers to a leadership position.; [minor] The summary mentions that Amasai 'may possibly be identical with Amasa, one of David's commanders'. This is an interesting detail, but Amasa was primarily known as Absalom's commander (2 Sam 17:25), whom David later forgave and appointed. The wording should be clarified to avoid misunderstandings.; [major] Verses 1, 2, 14, 15 in 1 Chronicles 12 do not directly concern Amasai. Verses 1-2 deal with Benjaminite warriors who came to David at Ziklag, and verses 14-15 concern the Gadites. Amasai is specifically mentioned in verse 18. This event should either be revised with correct verses or removed, as it partially overlaps with other events.; [minor] Verse 19 in 1 Chronicles 12 actually concerns some from Manasseh who defected to David, not directly about David receiving Amasai's group. It is verse 18b that describes David receiving them. Verse 19 should be removed from this reference.; [minor] Amasai also had a prophetic function in that the Spirit came upon him and he spoke inspired words. The role of 'prophetic spokesperson' or similar could be considered.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. There are several interesting details about Amasai that deserve footnotes, including the linguistic meaning of his name, the possible identification with Amasa, and the theological significance of the Spirit coming upon him.

versions.summary: Amasai was the leader of a group of warriors who came to David in Ziklag while he was fleeing from King Saul. The Holy Spirit came upon Amasai, and he declared loyalty to David with inspired words: "We are yours, David! Peace, peace be with you and with your helpers! For your God helps you." He is counted among David's foremost supporters in the struggle for the kingdom. Some scholars have suggested that he may be identical to Amasa, who later became Absalom's army commander (2 Sam 17:25), but this is disputed.
versions.title: Leader of the Thirty Warriors
versions.reason: [minor] The title "Leader of the Thirty Warriors" is somewhat imprecise. The text in 1 Chr 12:18 states that Amasai was "chief of the thirty" (or "leader of the captains"), but it is uncertain whether this refers to the same elite group "the thirty" mentioned in 2 Sam 23 and 1 Chr 11. A more accurate title would be "Leader of the Warriors Who Came to David".; [minor] The summary is good, but the quoted statement from Amasai contains a slight omission compared to the biblical text. In 1 Chr 12:18, the phrase "We are with you, son of Jesse!" is also included – this appears in the keyEvents description but is missing from the summary quote. Consistency should be maintained.; [minor] The reference to Amasa and 2 Sam 17:25 in the summary is interesting, but it may make the summary unnecessarily speculative. This information fits better as a footnote (where it is already covered). The summary should focus more on Amasai's own role and significance.; [minor] The first key event states that the warriors came "from the tribes of Benjamin and Judah". The text in 1 Chr 12:16 specifically mentions men from Benjamin and Judah, but Amasai's tribal affiliation is somewhat unclear. The wording is acceptable but should be clarified slightly.; [minor] The two key events overlap significantly – verse 18 is included in both. They could have been combined into one more comprehensive event, or the first event could have been limited to verses 16–17 to avoid the overlap.; [minor] The second footnote regarding the identification of Amasai with Amasa should be classified as "historical" rather than "theological", since it concerns a historical-critical identification of persons.; [minor] The third footnote on "the Spirit clothed himself" should be classified as "linguistic" rather than "theological", as it primarily discusses a Hebrew expression and its parallels.

versions.summary: Amasai was the leader of a group of warriors from Benjamin and Judah who came to David in Ziklag while he was fleeing from King Saul. The Holy Spirit came upon Amasai, and he declared loyalty to David with inspired, poetic words: "We are yours, David! We stand with you, son of Jesse! Peace, peace be with you, and peace with your helpers! For your God helps you." David received them and gave them leadership roles among his warriors. Amasai appears in the text as a man who was seized by God's Spirit at a decisive moment, and his words of loyalty marked an important turning point in the support for David's kingdom.
versions.title: Leader of the warriors who joined David
versions.reason: [minor] The description states that the warriors came to David 'at the stronghold of Ziklag'. In 1 Chr 12:16-17, the context is that they came to David, but the text does not explicitly mention 'the stronghold'. Ziklag was a city, not a fortress. It is better to say that they came to David at Ziklag without adding 'the stronghold'.; [minor] The summary is good, but it closely resembles the two previous versions in structure and wording (starting with 'Amasai was the leader of a group of warriors ... came to David at Ziklag while he was fleeing from King Saul'). It should be rephrased more distinctly to set it apart from earlier versions.; [minor] Verse 18 covers the Spirit coming upon Amasai and his words of loyalty, but verse 19 (in some numbering systems) or the latter part of verse 18 mentions that David received them and gave them leadership roles. It may be worth including verse 19 for completeness, since the description also notes that David appointed them as leaders.

footnotes.text: The name Amasai (Hebrew: עֲמָשַׂי, 'Amasay') is derived from the root עמס meaning "to bear" or "to load." The name can be interpreted as "burdensome" or "the one who bears."

The identification of Amasai with Amasa (2 Sam 17:25) is debated among scholars. Some believe they are the same person based on the similarity of their names and chronological placement, while others see them as two different individuals. Amasa was the son of Jether and Abigail, David's sister, and was appointed army commander by Absalom during his rebellion against David.

The expression "the Spirit clothed himself with Amasai" (Hebrew: רוּחַ לָבְשָׁה) is a rare formulation in the Old Testament, also used concerning Gideon (Judg 6:34) and Zechariah (2 Chr 24:20). The verb לָבַשׁ ("to clothe oneself") used with the Spirit of God as subject indicates a special divine empowerment to speak prophetically.

Ziklag was a city in the Negev region that Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, gave to David as a place of refuge (1 Sam 27:6). Archaeological excavations at possible sites for Ziklag (including Tell esh-Sharia and Khirbet Ziklag) have uncovered traces of settlement from the Iron Age that correspond with the biblical period.

"The Thirty" (Hebrew: הַשְּׁלֹשִׁים) was a designation for an elite group of warriors in David's military organization. The group is mentioned in 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11, and formed the core of David's military leadership. Whether Amasai belonged specifically to this group or led another force of thirty men remains somewhat unclear from the text.

Amasai's prophetic words of loyalty in 1 Chr 12:18 follow a poetic pattern with parallelism, typical of Hebrew poetry. The words "Peace, peace be with you" (שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם) use repetition for emphasis, a common rhetorical figure in biblical Hebrew.

In 1 Chronicles 12, several groups of warriors who joined David at various stages of his time as an outlaw and later as king are presented. The context shows that the joining of warriors from different tribes—including Benjamin, Saul's own tribe—was a theological sign that God's will pointed toward David as Israel's rightful king.
